text: One evening. <break time="0.8s" /> Keawe met a beautiful young woman. <break time="0.8s" /> Named Kokua by the road. <break time="0.8s" /> And before they parted. <break time="0.8s" /> She agreed to marry him. <break time="0.8s" /> Keawe rode home singing with joy. <break time="0.8s" /> But that night. <break time="0.8s" /> As he got ready for his bath. <break time="0.8s" /> He saw a strange spot on his skin. <break time="0.8s" /> It was the Chinese Evil. <break time="0.8s" /> A terrible sickness. <break time="0.8s" /> For which there was no cure. <break time="0.8s" /> In those days. <break time="0.8s" /> People with this sickness. <break time="0.8s" /> Had to leave their families. <break time="0.8s" /> And live apart. <break time="0.8s" /> On the island of Molokai. <break time="0.8s" /> If I had not sold the bottle. <break time="0.8s" /> I could have wished this sickness away. <break time="0.8s" /> Thought Keawe with a heavy heart. <break time="0.8s" /> It was not the house but Kokua. <break time="0.8s" /> That he could not give up. <break time="0.8s" /> So he decided. <break time="0.8s" /> To find the bottle again. <break time="0.8s" /> He sailed to Honolulu. <break time="0.8s" /> Where he learned that Lopaka had sold it. <break time="0.8s" /> And that it had passed from hand to hand. <break time="0.8s" /> At last he found it with a young man. <break time="0.8s" /> In Beritania Street. <break time="0.8s" /> Who had paid only two cents for it. <break time="0.8s" /> I am sorry for you. <break time="0.8s" /> Said the young man. <break time="0.8s" /> For one cent is the smallest coin. <break time="0.8s" /> And you can never sell it again. <break time="0.8s" /> Still Keawe bought it for one cent. <break time="0.8s" /> And the moment he made his wish. <break time="0.8s" /> His skin became clean and healthy.
